title: Off Broadway Review: NO SINGING IN THE NAVY - Bored and Confused?

Kramer, Celik, and all three actors have a connection that goes back to San Diego. The show then made its way to New York for this off-Broadway premiere, running March 18th through April 19th in the Peter Jay Sharp Theater. In the program, Kramer writes about the inspiration behind the piece. This was very interesting. It's this idea of the sailor as an American cultural icon. These cheerful, wide-eyed boys in white hats from musicals like On the Town or those old movie musicals. This image is idealistic, innocent, American masculinity, and Kramer was asking, "What does it mean that we celebrate that image while completely ignoring the fact that these sailors are part of an imperialistic military machine." As Kramer put it in press notes, it's a quote, "a doomed optimism scrubbed clean of detail. I'm this happy, innocent, masculine, sexy baby, and I'm about to die." End quote. Our three sailors, played by Bailey Lee, Eliana Nikbakht, and Elliot Sagay, are all making their off-Broadway debuts, and they have just arrived in the big city with a hundred bucks and 24 hours of leave before they are shipped off to war and to almost certain death. Sound familiar? Yes, it's very much in the spirit of On the Town. That's the basic template. But here's where it gets fun and weird. Early on in the play, the sailors encounter a crab, an actual character, who has escaped from a crab bucket and runs into them. And she teaches them how to sing. And this is a problem because the captain has one rule, and that is no singing in the navy. The subtext, shall we say, is rich. Though none of the lyrics spell it out, which means a child could watch this show and not bat an eye. Now, this is a musical, but it's not a musical in the traditional sense, where you have dialogue and then it breaks into a 3-minute fully crafted song with a verse, a chorus, and a button. The writing operates kind of like a stream of consciousness that's set to music. The sailors speak in rhythm, they move in and out of song, and the music ranges from sparse, sometimes just a foot stomp or a single chord, to full-on grooves. It's playful, it's messy, but in the best way, and it's very theatrical. And it's directed with such a broad presentational energy by A Sank Celik that every choice feels deliberately joyful and big. The set design is very minimal. It's a piano, a clothing rack, and those Mylar reflective strips that are surrounding the space and shimmering like water. It's simple, it's evocative, and it works great for this kind of off-the-cuff piece. So, let me talk about what works and what gave me pause. What works? Almost everything, honestly. The direction by A Sank Celik is terrific. The three performers are committed, they're loose, they're clearly having a great time. The conceptual underpinning interrogating the golden age of American innocence and its relationship to military violence is smart and very timely. Kramer has a genuine and singular voice, and there's something quietly radical about making a piece this silly that's also this pointed. Other critics have noticed that Kramer's work has this quality of being at once a deeply generous and deeply skeptical. It's warm and subversive in the same breath, and that's very much what's on display here. And it's very childlike, which is disarming. And honestly, it's just a lot of fun. Genuinely, purely fun. At 90 minutes, it's running right up against its limit. I loved it, but I was also ready for it to wrap up. This show establishes its premise in the very first moment.
